He limped down the bank to the culvert mouth, staff levelled at the dark arch, and called out — a rough shout that went echoing off the bricks and under the road.

Mud sucked at his boots as he came to the ditch. The smell was stronger here, dog and old bones and stagnant water. His shout came back at him from the stone throat, and for a breath nothing answered.

Then gravel shifted in the dark. A shape slid out of the culvert's mouth low and fast — the third hound, leaner than the others, ribs like barrel staves, mud to the elbows. It cleared the ditch in one scramble and stood on the road's edge not five paces from him, head dropped between its shoulders, a growl building in its chest like a saw drawn slow across wood.

It looked at him. It looked at the smoking body by the kiln mouth. The growl climbed.

Then it sprang — jaws opening, all teeth — coming at him over the mud.

The passage back led through the brokerage room — Tam's lamp was out now, the counter dark — and up a narrow stair at the back of the main hall. Light showed under a door at the head of the stairs, marked with a chalked sigil.

Inside, a lean man with close-cropped white hair sat at a desk sorting stone tiles into trays — Skill Stones, each one dark and smooth, though most of the trays sat nearly empty. He looked up over his spectacles.

"Lessons this late? You've caught the tail of the day, no more." He set down the stone he was holding. He tapped a second tray. "That one's four silver, stone and lesson together. The rest of my stock went out this morning, so it's that or come back in three days when the caravan from Crownheart arrives."

dawn.text:
Grey light came through the shutter slats, and the room was cold enough to see his breath. Two of the other cots stood empty already; someone below was hauling a barrow over cobblestones with a squeaking wheel.

He lay still and did the thing he had learned to do, turning his attention inward the way one probes a sore tooth — and there it was, sitting behind his breastbone alongside the bolt and the ward: the Lance. Not a memory of the drilling but the working itself, settled and named, as much a part of him now as the scar on his knuckle. The fire that answered surer at the kiln yard, the black line bitten into the plaster — it had all been real, and the proof of it lived in him where only he could look.

He also felt, in the same quiet accounting, what the day before had cost: the ache in his side where the hounds had gotten to him, and the hollow, thin feeling of his mana, still part-spent. Sleep had taken the edge off neither entirely. That, too, was simply true when he looked.

Downstairs, the broad innkeeper was already at his rag and his bar, and the smell of something frying came from the kitchen behind him.

price.text:
Tanners' Row announced itself before the first shop sign did. The smell came down the side street in layers — lime and dung and something sour that sat at the back of the throat — and Alaric walked it past tanning yards where hides hung pale as laundry over frames, and pit men in leather aprons worked the vats with long poles. A cart of wet skins went by, dripping a brown trail. One of the yards had a boy posted at the gate with a stick, shooing dogs; he looked Alaric over, decided he was no dog, and went back to his whittling.

The first apothecary had a painted sign, a polished front window, and prices to match, if the tidy display of glass vials on a velvet runner said anything. The second sat two doors down: a crooked wooden board with a mortar and pestle carved on it, a window fogged by a drying rack of herbs hung just inside, and a door that stuck before it gave.

Inside it smelled of camphor and vinegar. Bundles hung from every beam — willow bark, something blue-flowered, something Alaric didn't want to guess at — and shelves of clay pots and squat bottles lined the wall behind a counter scarred with knife marks. A woman in a stained grey smock sat at a small table near the back, grinding something in a stone mortar, unhurried. She looked up, took in the robes and the staff, and said, "Guild or temple?"

She set the pestle down when Alaric said what he wanted.

"Mana draught, small vial." She went along the shelf, pulled two bottles, and set them on the counter. "This one's my own brew — five silver. Clean, mild taste, works inside the hour. Lasts, too." She tapped the second bottle, darker and cloudier. "That one I bought off a carter who trades up from Crownheart. Three silver. Stronger going down — I'll say that kindly. I can't vouch for it past that."

She folded her arms. "Which is it to be? Or were you wanting something else besides?"
